# Workflow  

A standard workflow for approaching survival analysis is given below. This will change for any given analysis, but forms a useful starting point. 


## Exploratory Analysis  

1. **Check number of failures is sufficient**: For each level of categorical variables to be included in the model there should usually be a minimum of about 10. If there are not sufficient for one level of a category, it may be possible to rectify this by merging categories, but only with the guidance of a subject matter expert. 

2. **Plot the distribution of continuous predictors:** This is typically achieved through histograms or other univariate methods. Highly skewed distributions may be good candidates for transformations. It is also useful to check for associations between variables using cross tabulation, scatterplots etc.  


## Kaplan-Meier Plots

As an exploratory technique, Kaplan-Meier plots can be made for the entire marginal survival data, however there is significant benefit in stratifying these plots by the categorical variables in your data. Furthermore, continuous variables can be discretized into 2 or 3 levels and the Kaplan-Meier curves compared. 


## Model Building    

Some authors suggest a step-wise process for model fitting. These methods should be used with caution and a deeper appreication for the scientific merics of including/excluding variables, and not as a dogmatic exercise. The following guide is adapted from @hosmer2008applied: 

1. Conduct univariate analysis to detect significant differences in survival curves for each variable.  

2. Fit a multivariable model containing all variables significant in the univariable analysis at the 20-25 percent level.  

3. Use the p-values from the Wald tests of the individual coefficients to identify covariates that might be deleted from the model.    

4. Following the fit of the reduced model, we assess whether removal of the covariate has produced an 'important' change in the coefficients of the variables remaining in the model. If the variable excluded is an important confounder, it should be added back into the model. This process continues until no covariates can be deleted from the model.  

5. At this point, we add to the model, one at a time, all variables excluded from the initial multivariable model to confirm that they are neither statistically significant nor an important confounder.

5. Test for the addition of more complex interaction terms.  

## Diagnostics

- Check proportional hazards and modify model if required. A useful measures to control for violation of the proportional hazards assumption is to stratify by the offending variable. 

- Check diagnostics for final model:  
  - Proportional hazards
  - Cox-Snell  
  - dfBeta    

## Outputs  

1. Predicted survival curves  
2. Tabulated hazard rates

## Workflow Diagram  

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[(survival data)] --> X[Exploratory Analysis]
  X[Exploratory Analysis]--> B[Kaplan-Meier Estimator]
  B --> C[Log Rank Test]  
  C --> D[Cox Proportional Hazards Model]
  C -.-> E[Fully parametric model]  
  D --> G[Diagnostics & Model Fitting]
  G --> D
  
  
  style D fill:#f9f
```

# End to End Case Study  

For patients with advanced lung cancer from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group, how does age and sex effect survival?  

```{r}
library(survival) 
library(ggsurvfit)
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(broom)
library(knitr)

data(cancer)

lung_df <- lung |> 
  select(time, status, age, sex) |> 
  mutate(
    status = status-1,
    age_cat = cut(age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 70, 90))
    )


head(lung_df)
table(lung_df$status)
skim(lung_df)

hist(lung_df$time)
hist(lung_df$age)

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung_df) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, color = "gray50") +
  scale_ggsurvfit()

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung_df) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, color = "gray50") +
  scale_ggsurvfit()

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ age_cat, data = lung_df) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, color = "gray50") +
  scale_ggsurvfit()


survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung_df)


fit <- coxph(
  Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age,
  data = lung_df
)

summary(fit)

tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

cox.zph(fit)

# Survival curve for a 60-year-old female (sex=2) 
new_patient <- data.frame(age = c(65), sex = c(1, 2))

cox_surv <- survfit(fit, newdata = new_patient)
cox_surv
plot(cox_surv, xlab = "Days", ylab = "S(t)", main = "Covariate-adjusted survival")


```
